title: Bernoulli's Equation

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

expression: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant   (along a streamline)
explanation: Bernoulli's equation is a statement of energy conservation (work-energy theorem applied to fluid flow) for an ideal fluid — incompressible, non-viscous, and undergoing steady, streamline (laminar) flow. As a fluid speeds up (per the continuity equation A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ in a narrowing pipe), pressure must drop to keep the sum constant, and vice versa; height changes also trade off against pressure and speed.

variables.meaning: Pressure at a point in the fluid

workedExample.scenario: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows, speeding up from 1 m/s to 4 m/s.
workedExample.substitution: P1 + ½ρ(1)² = P2 + ½ρ(4)² (same height, h cancels)
workedExample.result: P1 − P2 = ½ρ(16−1) = 7.5ρ, so pressure drops significantly where the fluid speeds up

commonMistakes: Applying Bernoulli's equation to a real, viscous, or turbulent flow and expecting exact results — its idealised assumptions (non-viscous, incompressible, streamline) don't strictly hold in such cases.
Believing higher speed always means higher pressure — Bernoulli's equation shows the OPPOSITE: at the same height, higher speed corresponds to LOWER pressure.
genZNote: Bernoulli's whole deal: speed and pressure are in a strict trade-off, never both high at once.
